summary.text: The cover, copyright page and table of contents of Module 13 of the WHO implementation tool for HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), on integrating STI services, listing sections for programme managers and health workers and annexes on pathogens and testing guidance.

blocks.title: Introduction to the WHO PrEP implementation tool
blocks.content:
1	 HIV acquisition risk varies considerably within populations and geographical locations. Population-level HIV incidence is an important determinant of individual-level risk 
of HIV acquisition. However, when considering who could benefit from PrEP, it is important to take into account the characteristics and behaviours of individuals and their 
partners that could lead to HIV exposure. Even in locations with a low overall HIV incidence, there may be individuals at substantial risk who could benefit from PrEP services. 
Individuals requesting PrEP should be given priority to be offered PrEP s

summary.text: Introduces the WHO PrEP implementation tool, developed after WHO's 2015 recommendation to offer oral PrEP to people at substantial HIV risk. It stresses that individual risk varies, that people requesting PrEP should be prioritized, that barriers faced by key populations should be addressed and that the choice to use PrEP rests with the individual.

blocks.title: Audience and scope of the tool
blocks.content:
The HIV PrEP implementation tool contains modules for a range of stakeholders to support them in the consideration, 
planning, introduction, implementation and roll-out of PrEP. The modules can be used on their own or in combination. 
In addition, there is a module for individuals interested in or already taking oral PrEP.
This module does not make any new recommendations. It compiles existing WHO recommendations, systematic scientific 
literature reviews and other relevant publications to provide suggested implementation approaches. It is the product of 
collaboration among many experts, comm

summary.text: Explains that the PrEP tool is a set of modules for different stakeholders and that this STI integration module compiles existing WHO guidance without making new recommendations.

blocks.title: Guiding principles
blocks.content:
It is important to adopt an evidence-based public health, human rights, and people- and community-centred approach when 
offering PrEP. Such an approach is aligned with principles of universal health coverage, gender equality and health-related 
rights, including accessibility, availability, acceptability and quality of services for people who need PrEP. Placing the people 
and communities who could benefit from PrEP at the centre allows services to be adapted to their preferences and needs to 
attain sexual health.
According to WHO’s definition (5), sexual health is:
“…a state of physical, em

summary.text: Sets out guiding principles for offering PrEP through a public health, human rights and people-centred approach and quotes WHO's definition of sexual health.

blocks.title: The module on PrEP and STI service integration
blocks.content:
Many bacteria, viruses and parasites 
are known to be transmitted 
through sexual contact. Some have 
a major impact on sexual, 
reproductive and neonatal health 
and can result in severe or life-
threatening complications if not 
detected and treated in a timely 
manner (see Box 1).
Box 1. Examples of infections that can be transmitted through sexual contact and can have serious 
consequences for sexual health and well-being
•	 Vertical transmission of syphilis can result in stillbirth, neonatal death, low birth weight, and prematurity and congenital 
deformities.
•	 Human papillomavirus (HPV

summary.text: Introduces the module on integrating STI services with PrEP and lists in a box serious consequences of sexually transmitted infections such as congenital syphilis, HPV-related cancers, infertility and chronic hepatitis.

blocks.title: Epidemiology of STIs
blocks.content:
In 2020 there were approximately 374 million estimated 
incident cases of four curable STIs – syphilis, caused by 
Treponema pallidum (6 million cases); gonorrhoea, 
caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae (87 million cases); 
Chlamydia trachomatis (127 million cases); and 
Trichomonas vaginalis (156 million cases) (6). (6,7).
Syphilis during pregnancy caused an estimated annual 661 000 cases of congenital syphilis, including over 200 000 fetal 
and neonatal deaths (2016 estimate) (8). Almost 500 million adults were estimated to be living with genital herpes globally 
in 2016 (9); and HPV was responsi

summary.text: Gives global figures for curable STIs, estimating 374 million new cases in 2020, along with congenital syphilis, genital herpes and HPV-related cervical cancer, most occurring in low- and middle-income countries. It also explains that the module has two parts, for programme managers and for facility managers and health workers.

blocks.title: High burden of STIs and associated factors among people on HIV PrEP
blocks.content:
A systematic review of the STI burden among people accessing PrEP, predominantly men who have sex with men, showed 
that STI prevalence prior to starting PrEP was high (12% for gonorrhoea, 11% for chlamydia, 5% for active syphilis and 24% 
for any of the three). STI incidence remained high at follow-up visits for PrEP refills (11). For comparison, the estimated 
global prevalence in 2020 of these STIs among persons assigned male at birth, ages 15–49 years, was 0.7% for gonorrhoea, 
2.5% for chlamydia and 0.6% for syphilis (6). For viral hepatitis, a global systematic review showed that among m

summary.text: Reviews evidence that STI prevalence and incidence are high among people on PrEP, including men who have sex with men and young African women, compared with general population estimates. It discusses contributing factors such as sexual networks, condom use, stigma and background prevalence.

blocks.title: Why integrate STI services?
blocks.content:
Offering STI services to PrEP clients creates an important opportunity for people to benefit from such services who 
otherwise may not access STI testing and treatment, particularly those at high risk of infection and are asymptomatic 
(28,29). Integrating STIs services into PrEP services, as well as offering PrEP to people seeking STI and related services, 
fosters synergies and efficiencies in the public health response to HIV and STIs. Of equal importance, it also promotes a 
people-centred approach (30) 1 to improve sexual health and quality of care, and it creates opportunities to build t

summary.text: Explains the reasons for integrating STI services into PrEP, including reaching people with asymptomatic infections, efficiency gains, people-centred care and tackling antimicrobial resistance in gonorrhoea. It links integration to global targets for reducing STIs, congenital syphilis and cervical cancer deaths by 2030.

blocks.content: Photograph of a hand in a blue laboratory glove holding a Petri dish with bacterial colonies streaked on red agar.

blocks.title: Part 1. Integration of STI services for programme managers and other decision-makers
blocks.content: and other decision-makers

summary.text: A section heading for Part 1 of the module, on integration of STI services for programme managers and other decision-makers.

blocks.title: Planning for integration
blocks.content:
Differentiated service delivery (DSD) is a person-centred approach that simplifies and adapts PrEP and STI services to meet 
clients’ needs and situations (2). DSD can ensure that the health system functions efficiently, enable the health system to 
focus resources on those most in need and, most importantly, enhance client outcomes.
Considering the WHO DSD framework (35) and its adaptation for the provision of PrEP (2), when planning for the integration 
of STI services, public health officials need to decide which STI services will be offered, how they will be offered, who will 
offer them a

summary.text: Describes using the differentiated service delivery framework to plan which STI services to integrate with PrEP, and how, by whom and where they are offered.

blocks.title: How to integrate STI services?
blocks.content:
A stepwise approach to the integration of STI services with PrEP services should be considered (Fig. 2). This approach should 
be informed by the local context, including epidemiology, availability of resources and acceptability to users and health care 
workers. When the information is available, the cost-effectiveness of the different levels of STI services provided should be 
considered.
Through this stepwise approach, programmes can transition from clinical management of STIs based on signs and symptoms 
to services based on etiologic management and can focus on enhancing access to STI int

summary.text: Recommends a stepwise approach to integrating STI services with PrEP, adapted to local context and moving from symptom-based to cause-based management.

blocks.title: What STI services to integrate?
blocks.content:
Although it is not currently feasible to offer STI services to all people on PrEP everywhere, the gradual addition of services 
using a stepwise approach can encourage and advance integration of STI services. Particular STI services will need to be 
adapted to PrEP service delivery models (from digital health/virtual interventions (36,37) to facility-based models with 
laboratory infrastructure) as well as to the local context. See Annex 2 for examples of STI services that might be offered 
with different models of PrEP delivery.

summary.text: Explains that STI services should be added gradually and adapted to each PrEP delivery model, from digital to facility-based, with examples in an annex.

blocks.title: Where to integrate STI services?
blocks.content:
Currently, programmes offer PrEP through a variety of service delivery models. The STI services selected for integration 
should be feasible for the specific model of PrEP delivery as well as aligned with local resources, laws and regulations. 
Annex 2 also provides examples of different combinations of STI services and where and how they can be offered to people 
who use PrEP.

summary.text: Notes that STI services chosen for integration must suit the PrEP delivery model and local resources, laws and regulations.

blocks.title: Who should offer integrated services?
blocks.content:
As a range of health care workers may deliver PrEP, including trained peers and other lay providers, task shifting and task 
sharing are important to PrEP and STI service integration and scale-up (38). Along with increasing access, they may generate 
health system efficiencies and support models of service provision that are more acceptable to people on PrEP.

summary.text: Discusses which health workers can deliver integrated PrEP and STI services, stressing task sharing with peers and lay providers, and shows a stepwise diagram from syndromic management to testing and vaccination. A case study describes integrated PrEP and STI services for key populations at a government health centre in Phnom Penh, Cambodia.

Photograph of a health worker in a mask showing a box of tablets to a client through a service window; the client, also masked, is seen from behind.

blocks.title: Human resources and capacity building
blocks.content:
The human resources required to offer STI services to people who 
access PrEP will vary according to the characteristics of existing PrEP 
delivery models, including but not limited to the different cadres of 
health care workers, the possibility of task sharing and task shifting 
(38), engagement of peer and community health care workers, as well 
as local laws and regulations on the qualifications required to provide 
specific services. It is likely that additional human resources may be needed. As with any health service provision, there will 
be a need to establish or include STI services

summary.text: Describes the staffing and training needed to add STI services to PrEP delivery, such as training on diagnostic algorithms, case management and antimicrobial resistance. It also outlines the role of peers and community workers in linking clients to care and supporting adherence.

blocks.title: Costs
blocks.content:
Integrating the delivery of PrEP and STI services can increase efficiency in the use of national resources. Furthermore, 
considering that, historically, HIV programmes are fairly well-funded, offering integrated STI services to people on PrEP 
creates an opportunity to leverage additional funding and resources for the STI response, which typically is underfunded.
It is critical for PrEP programmes to consider a range of STI-related interventions, including, for example, testing and 
treatment of syphilis, despite the additional investment that integration often requires, particularly for pers

summary.text: Argues that integrating PrEP and STI services can improve efficiency and draw HIV funding into the underfunded STI response, while noting extra costs for staff, training and supplies. It highlights the cost-effectiveness of dual HIV/syphilis tests and presents a Pan American Health Organization costing tool with an example comparing budget scenarios for 2021–2025.

blocks.title: Documentation, monitoring and evaluation
blocks.content:
Documentation, monitoring and evaluation of the provision of STI services 
for people on PrEP are essential to assess service performance and adjust 
interventions in a timely manner. For countries that do not have a system 
that can capture STI data, monitoring questions related to STIs can be 
incorporated into existing PrEP-related reporting systems (for example, 
sexual history taking) and do not need to be developed independently. This 
will allow the longitudinal follow-up of users diagnosed with an STI and 
tracking of regular check-ups.
It is critical to ensure the 
confidentiality of

summary.text: Stresses documenting and monitoring STI services for PrEP users within existing reporting systems while protecting confidentiality, and points to suggested indicators. A case study from Namibia describes an online platform used to promote testing and manage HIV and STI services for key populations.

blocks.content: Infographic titled 'Using QuickRes to book appointments for STI services in Namibia' showing three smartphone screens. The first is an IntraHealth Namibia social media post ('All our STI & HIV health services are FREE'), captioned 'Simple social media promotions bring clients to QuickRes'; the second is a risk assessment result page ('Time to act!'), captioned 'The Risk Assessment tool helps clients to decide what services to choose'; the third lists clinics and their services, captioned 'Clients can choose their preferred provider, date and time for their appointment'.
Colourful digital illustration of a person with blue skin, dark wavy hair and pink sunglasses, wearing an orange hooded sweatshirt.

blocks.title: Demand generation for STI services among people accessing PrEP
blocks.content:
Like demand generation for HIV PrEP (see WHO PrEP implementation tool Module 2: community educators and advocates 
(48)), creating demand for STI services is critical. It can raise awareness of STI signs and symptoms and potential exposure 
to an STI, as well as promote care-seeking behaviours such as regular STI testing and notifying partners of an STI diagnosis. 
This is particularly relevant as most STIs do not present signs or symptoms and can be easily cured.
It also is critical to engage with communities when planning demand generation activities 
so that messaging is based on their need

summary.text: Explains the need to generate demand for STI services among PrEP users, since most STIs are asymptomatic, and to involve communities in designing messages. A case study describes a Brazilian project that used social media and a chatbot to reach adolescents from key populations.

blocks.title: Preparing for upcoming innovations
blocks.content:
Upcoming innovations may make the provision of integrated PrEP and STI services more efficient and acceptable and 
support scale-up. Currently, WHO does not have recommendations on these innovations. As evidence becomes available, 
WHO guidelines will be released.
•	 Innovations in STI testing
o	 Syphilis self-test and HIV/syphilis self-test. Self-tests 
have proved highly acceptable to both health care workers 
and clients, and WHO recommendations already exist for 
HIV and hepatitis C. WHO is currently working towards 
having recommendations also for self-tests for syphilis 
and for dual HIV

summary.text: Describes upcoming innovations that may ease integrated PrEP and STI services, including syphilis and dual HIV/syphilis self-tests, rapid tests for active syphilis and multiplex point-of-care platforms. It also mentions prevention innovations and vaccines and tests in development, noting WHO has not yet issued recommendations on them.

blocks.content: Photograph of four people sitting together outdoors in front of a brick building, talking and smiling.

blocks.title: Part 2. STI service delivery for facility managers and health care workers
blocks.content:
care workers
As mentioned in Part 1, different STI services can be integrated with PrEP services 
depending on how and where PrEP is offered and on local resources. Fig. 4 summarizes 
an optimal package of STI services that could be integrated at the facility level with 
laboratory support. In all contexts, however, inability to offer STI services should never 
delay or be a barrier to the provision of PrEP nor to adopting strategies to simplify access 
to PrEP, such as making it available through pharmacies or home delivery.
Certain populations, such as adolescents and trans and gender divers

summary.text: Opens Part 2 for facility managers and health workers, presenting an optimal package of STI services that can be integrated with PrEP and stressing that lack of STI services must never delay PrEP. It highlights the specific needs of adolescents and trans and gender diverse people and includes a schematic of STI case management.

blocks.title: Providing information and promoting health-seeking behaviours
blocks.content:
During the first encounter with health services, clients should be provided with basic information on STIs (see Annex 4), including 
self-assessment for signs and symptoms (see example in Box 5) and prevention strategies (see section on STI Prevention).
Additionally, due to the intense stigma associated with 
STIs, clients should know that some symptoms associated 
with STIs can be caused by other, non-STI-related 
pathogens or conditions (Box 6). Also, reminding users 
that STI infection can be asymptomatic is critical.
STI-related information, such as that in Annex 4 and Box 5, 
can be provi

summary.text: Advises giving PrEP clients basic STI information, including self-assessment of symptoms, and reminding them that PrEP does not protect against other STIs. It notes that some symptoms have non-STI causes, such as candidiasis and bacterial vaginosis.

blocks.content: Photograph of a smiling health worker in a white uniform in a pharmacy store room, holding a box of tablets, with shelves of medicine boxes behind her.

blocks.title: Counselling
blocks.content:
Quality counselling is an essential component of client-centred care. Counselling is defined here as a non-judgemental 
interactive process between a trained health care worker or lay provider and a client during which information is exchanged 
and support is provided so that clients can make informed decisions, design a plan and take action to improve their health 
(58).1 For example, some behaviours associated with increased risk for HIV and STIs, such as use of sex dating apps and 
chemsex, particularly among men who have sex with men, are becoming more frequent. It is important for those p

summary.text: Defines counselling as a non-judgemental exchange that helps clients make informed decisions, noting that WHO does not recommend counselling aimed at changing behaviour. A box describes higher-risk practices such as chemsex and use of dating apps.

blocks.title: Prompting for signs and symptoms of STIs
blocks.content:
Prompting clients to notice STI signs and symptoms they may have is essential to promote health-seeking behaviours and to 
provide appropriate STI services, and it can be conducted as a self-assessment (see example in Box 5).
1	 The definition for counselling used in this module is adapted from WHO’s Counselling for maternal and newborn health care: a handbook for building skills (58).
WHO does not recommend counselling to change 
people’s behaviours as it has been shown to be 
ineffective to reduce HIV/STI incidence.
SOUTH AFRICA
Prompting youth for STI symptoms
In South Africa the standard o

summary.text: Stresses prompting clients to recognize STI signs and symptoms through self-assessment. A case study from South Africa describes adding symptom screening and a sub-study of laboratory STI testing to PrEP services for young people.

blocks.content: Photograph of three young men, seen from behind, crouching and spray-painting colourful graffiti on an outdoor wall.

blocks.title: STI prevention
blocks.content:
Vaccines and condoms are the primary STI prevention tools (Table 1). In settings where voluntary medical male circumcision 
(VMMC) is recommended for HIV prevention, it also provides protection against some other STIs (63,64,65). Currently, WHO 
recommends post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for bacterial STIs only in the case of sexual assault/rape (66,67). 
Table 1. WHO recommendations for STI prevention
Vaccines
•	 Hepatitis A: WHO recommends vaccination for people at higher risk of contracting hepatitis A virus in 
low-endemicity settings, which includes men who have sex with men and people wh

summary.text: Summarizes WHO recommendations for STI prevention, mainly vaccines against hepatitis A, hepatitis B and HPV, and condoms with compatible lubricants. It notes the role of male circumcision and that post-exposure prophylaxis for bacterial STIs is recommended only after sexual assault.

blocks.content: Close-up photograph of gloved hands collecting a fingerprick blood sample into a thin capillary tube.

blocks.title: STI testing
blocks.content:
Some STIs can be diagnosed using etiologic laboratory methods, such as molecular tests. Etiologic diagnosis of syphilis is 
feasible in almost all settings. However, for other pathogens, etiologic diagnosis remains limited due to high costs. 
Alternatively, some STIs require the collection of samples and the culture of the pathogen under specific laboratory 
conditions, which also are not widely available.
On the other hand, rapid tests allow people to be tested at the point of care 
and be treated for STIs in a single visit, greatly decreasing the risk of loss to 
follow-up. Furthermore, rapi

summary.text: Explains the options for STI testing, from laboratory and culture methods to rapid point-of-care and self-tests, and points to WHO laboratory guidance and prequalified diagnostics.

blocks.title: Frequency of testing
blocks.content:
Optimal frequencies of STI testing vary by pathogen, population and epidemiologic context. Considering the WHO guidance 
for differentiated and simplified PrEP services, PrEP follow-up visits may vary between people on PrEP (2). For STIs, self-
testing and self-sampling can be used between or in place of some clinic visits. For example, services that require PrEP 
clients to return every three months for a PrEP refill and for HIV and STI testing could provide PrEP for six months in addition 
to HIV self-test and kits for the self-collection of samples for STI testing.
A recent systematic revie

summary.text: Discusses how often PrEP users should be tested for STIs, noting that self-testing and self-sampling can replace some visits and that evidence is insufficient for a general testing frequency. It suggests prioritizing regular testing for people at higher risk.

blocks.title: Considerations for syphilis testing and diagnosis
blocks.content:
Many people with syphilis do not have any symptoms or signs of infection, or health care providers may not notice signs and 
symptoms. Syphilis diagnosis is complex, usually requiring clients’ clinical and sexual history, physical examination and 
laboratory testing.
The most widely available tests for syphilis are based on serology. These can be of two types: treponemal and non-
treponemal tests.
•	 Treponemal tests, which encompass laboratory tests, rapid single syphilis tests and rapid dual HIV/syphilis tests, are 
highly sensitive. However, they do not distinguish between active infection

summary.text: Explains the complexity of diagnosing syphilis and the differences between treponemal and non-treponemal serological tests and their limitations. It mentions dual rapid tests that may help identify active infection.

blocks.title: Considerations for the diagnosis of gonorrhoea and chlamydia
blocks.content:
The costs of high-performance molecular POC tests for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis remain prohibitive for many 
low- and middle-income countries posing an important barrier to increase testing coverage. Still, POC platforms for 
molecular testing are increasingly available in these countries for the diagnosis of tuberculosis (TB) and could be used for 
some STIs to optimize use of resources and increase testing coverage.
The use of self-collected samples can be an additional strategy to overcome the high cost of molecular testing when it is 
feasible to transport samples to a central labo

summary.text: Discusses barriers to diagnosing gonorrhoea and chlamydia, such as the cost of molecular tests, and options like shared TB testing platforms and self-collected samples. It stresses sampling from the throat, rectum and genitals, citing studies showing many infections are missed otherwise, and includes a country example of pooled testing for key populations.

blocks.content: Photograph of a masked health worker in a white coat showing a tablet computer screen to a masked client seated beside him at a desk in a clinic room.

blocks.title: Partner services
blocks.content:
WHO recommends that providers offer assistance to clients who test positive for HIV to notify their partners and link them 
to care (40). Partner services’ strategies (such as assisted partner notification services) (see Box 8) are proven to be highly 
efficient and effective in detecting new cases and have already been adopted by several low- and middle-income countries. 
These strategies can also be used for STIs (84).
Furthermore, combining partner service strategies with dual rapid HIV/syphilis testing could yield a greater number of 
previously undetected and untreated syphilis infections

summary.text: Recommends offering partner services to people who test positive for HIV or STIs and describes strategies such as user referral, provider referral and contract referral, noting their effectiveness when combined with dual HIV/syphilis testing.

blocks.title: Consultation and physical examination
blocks.content:
To establish a correct diagnosis, the health care provider needs to ensure 
that there is a conducive environment to enable people to discuss their 
sexual history freely.
Taking a sexual and medical history is also central to providing quality PrEP 
and STI care, and it is an important component of people-centred care. 
Obtaining clients’ sexual history will help providers to gauge a person’s 
likelihood of being infected with an STI. Sexual history taking is described in 
detail in Module 3 of the PrEP implementation tool (85).
As with counselling, taking a sexual 
history should not be a re

summary.text: Stresses the need for a private, supportive setting where clients can talk openly about their sexual history, which helps judge STI risk in PrEP services, while noting that history-taking should not be a condition for getting PrEP or STI care.

blocks.content: Illustrated poster headed 'IMAGINE HELPING ALL THESE BUTTS', showing many cartoon figures seen from behind in jeans, skirts and shorts standing on a map of North America, with flags reading 'Check me out!', 'My bottom is at the top of my list!' and 'My butt is getting the attention it deserves!'. The logo 'the ANCHOR study.org' appears at the bottom.

blocks.title: Physical examination

summary.text: Sets out how to prepare for and conduct a respectful physical examination for STIs, with consent, privacy, a chaperone and the option of self-collected samples, and lists what to look for in the mouth, skin, genitals and anal area. A case study from Nigeria describes donor-supported cryotherapy for anogenital warts in one-stop clinics for key populations and the cost and liquid nitrogen problems that threaten its sustainability.

blocks.content: Photograph of a masked, gloved health worker in a clinic room holding an instrument beside an examination couch, where a client lies covered by a white sheet.

blocks.title: Syndromic approach
blocks.content:
The syndromic approach identifies consistent groups of 
symptoms and easily recognized signs (syndromes –for 
example, vaginal discharge, urethral discharge, genital ulcers, 
abdominal pain) and treats for the most likely organisms 
producing the syndrome.
Syndromic case management can result in both overtreatment, because there are other 
causes of syndromes not related to an STI, and undertreatment, as the majority of STIs 
are asymptomatic. Despite these shortcomings, syndromic case management remains 
an essential component for treating people with symptoms of STIs in settings without 
lab

summary.text: Explains the syndromic approach to STIs, which treats groups of symptoms for their most likely causes but can lead to both over- and undertreatment. It notes WHO's 2021 guideline recommends treatment based on molecular tests where possible and syndromic management where testing is limited, with flow charts for five syndromes.

blocks.title: Specific treatment for common STIs
blocks.content:
Correct and effective STI treatment should be provided 
and taken, ideally, on the day of first contact between 
clients and health care providers. Rapid treatment of 
sexual partners is also critical to avoid reinfection and to 
break the chain of transmission, which could include 
expedited partner treatment.
A client who is prescribed treatment for an STI should be counselled on medication information, risks and benefits, adverse 
reactions, dosing and adherence.
Standardized treatment protocols for STIs ensure appropriate treatment at all levels of health care services and help reduce 
the

summary.text: Calls for correct STI treatment ideally on the first visit, rapid treatment of partners and counselling on medicines and adherence, using standard protocols to limit antimicrobial resistance. It points to WHO treatment guidelines for chlamydia, herpes, gonorrhoea, syphilis, syphilis in pregnancy and HPV-related cervical lesions.

blocks.title: Clinical follow-up
blocks.content:
Follow-up is generally limited to those with persistent symptoms after a stipulated period after the recommended treatment. 
Clients may return for further assessment if the condition has not resolved or it has recurred. The health care provider will 
need to determine the reason for the user’s return to guide next steps (see Box 10).
Box 10. Reasons for STI treatment failure that need to be assessed to guide further treatment
•	 Adherence: such as a client failing to complete a 7-day or 21-day course of doxycycline for the treatment of chlamydia, 
including for lymphogranuloma venereum (LVG).

summary.text: Explains that clinical follow-up is mainly for people whose symptoms persist after treatment and lists reasons for treatment failure, such as poor adherence, reinfection, antimicrobial resistance and other untreated infections. Footnotes note that WHO is revising gonorrhoea treatment because of growing resistance.

blocks.title: Referrals and linkage to care
blocks.content:
Sometimes people diagnosed with an STI will need to be referred to another level of care. For example, someone with an 
abnormality in the anorectal area may need to be referred to a colorectal surgeon or oncologist or for diagnostic tests. Health 
care workers should be provided with clear and easily accessible information on referral and counter-referral mechanisms.1
However, when referring someone to another facility, it is 
critical to consider loss to follow-up due to individual, 
programmatic and environmental factors (see Box 2). Loss 
to follow-up results in poorer outcomes such as lon

summary.text: Discusses referral of people with STIs to other levels of care and the risk of losing them to follow-up, which makes same-day treatment especially valuable. It lists strategies to support linkage, such as non-judgemental and flexible services, self-collection, free care, peer support, digital tools and clear national policies. A case study from South Africa describes client preferences, showing most favour self-led STI services but some prefer provider-led care, so services should offer choice.

blocks.content: Photograph of two young women walking and laughing together on a street beside a fenced brick wall.

blocks.title: Outbreaks of STIs and other infections that can be sexually transmissible
blocks.content:
There has been an increase in outbreaks of syphilis, gonorrhoea 
(including extensive drug resistance (XDR)1 by gonococci), LVG 
and HIV, as well as other pathogens not classified as STIs but 
that are transmissible through sexual contact, reported mostly by 
high-income countries among men who have sex with men. The 
most recent outbreaks include those by Shigella flexneri, Shigella 
sonnei (including multidrug resistance2 and XDR), verocytotoxin-

summary.text: Describes rising outbreaks of syphilis, gonorrhoea including extensively drug-resistant strains, lymphogranuloma venereum, HIV and other sexually transmissible infections such as Shigella, E. coli, hepatitis A, B and C and monkeypox, reported mainly among men who have sex with men in high-income countries. A box sets out how monkeypox spreads, its symptoms and differential diagnosis, contact tracing and vaccination of contacts soon after exposure. It ends by warning against stigmatizing affected groups and noting that PrEP services can help detect and report surges in infections.
